INVESTMENT POLICY STATEMENT - Marcus and Elena Dragomirescu, adopted 10 January 2025.

Purpose: to set out how the family portfolio is managed and reviewed.
Objectives: grow capital ahead of inflation by 3% a year over rolling ten-year periods; fund school costs from 2030 and financial independence from 2045.
Time horizon: 15 years or more.
Strategic allocation: 60% global equities, 30% bonds, 10% alternatives and cash, rebalanced when any sleeve drifts by more than 5 percentage points.
Liquidity: a reserve equal to twelve months of household spending is held outside the portfolio.
Exclusions: no direct holdings in tobacco producers, thermal coal miners or controversial weapons manufacturers; funds with a recognised sustainability label are preferred where costs are comparable.
Constraints: no borrowing, no single holding above 10%, sterling base currency.
Benchmark: composite of global equity and sterling bond indices.
Review: formally each year and after any major change in circumstances.

MEETING NOTE - INITIAL DISCOVERY MEETING
Client: Tobias Hallworth (TH). Adviser: Daniel Finch (DF). Date: 21 January 2025, 10:00 to 11:40, Leeds office. Also present: Joanna Hallworth (JH) for the first half hour.

1. How the introduction came about
TH was referred by his accountant after his late father's estate was wound up last autumn. He has never used an adviser before and has run his own ISA through an online platform. He was open that he has 'no real plan' and wants someone to pull the pieces together. I explained how we work, the difference between the initial planning stage and the ongoing service, and that today's meeting is at our cost. He asked sensible questions about how we are paid and whether we are tied to any provider; I confirmed that we are independent and hold no client money.

2. Personal and family
TH is 43, married to JH (41), with two children: Felix (11) and Martha (8). Both adults are in good health; TH is a non-smoker and JH gave up five years ago. They have lived in Harrogate since 2018 and have no plans to move. Wills were written when Felix was born and have not been looked at since. Neither of them has a power of attorney in place and they had not heard of the idea before today.

3. Work
TH is Principal Data Engineer at Kestrel Ridge Analytics in Leeds, where he has been for almost six years. Basic of £75,000 plus a bonus that has paid out every year so far (the last one was about £11,000). He enjoys the job and expects to stay. JH is a part-time physiotherapist at a private clinic and earns roughly £24,000 a year, with hours that vary from month to month. Before Kestrel Ridge, TH spent nine years at Marlowe Steelworks and has a deferred pension in the old scheme there which he 'has not looked at for years'.

4. What they own and owe
The house is worth around £560,000, with a mortgage of about £231,000 with Lanchester Bank, fixed until the middle of 2028. They have a joint current account and an easy-access account holding roughly £38,000. TH's ISA is worth about £96,000, almost entirely in a single global tracker. His workplace pension is now inside a SIPP with Aviary Life, about £280,000. JH has an NHS pension from her earlier career and a small personal pension. The inheritance from his father, £684,000 after a few final bills, is sitting in a deposit account paying very little. No credit card balances are carried from month to month and there is no car finance.

5. What they want
In TH's words: 'not to mess up what Dad left us'. Specifically: (a) clear the mortgage, or decide deliberately not to; (b) be able to stop full-time work at 60; (c) see both children through university without them taking on large debts; (d) a bigger emergency pot now that JH's hours vary. JH added that she would like one family holiday a year ring-fenced 'so that we actually enjoy some of it'.

6. Paperwork received today
TH brought the originals we had asked for. He handed over his passport and a recent utility bill, which I copied, certified and returned to him before he left. JH did not have hers with her and will drop them in next week. TH will e-mail his last three payslips and his year-end tax certificate from work. A copy of the grant of probate is already with us, sent on by the accountant.

7. Feel for investment risk
A brief conversation only; the questionnaire is to be completed at home. TH describes himself as 'fairly relaxed' - he held his tracker through 2020 and 2022 without selling. JH is more cautious and does not want the whole sum in the markets at once. Phasing in over twelve months was mentioned as a possibility, as was keeping the amount needed for the mortgage out of shares altogether.

8. Things I noticed
They make decisions together and JH should be invited to every meeting, not just the first. Life cover exists on TH only (a term policy taken out in 2021); nothing on JH, and no income protection for either of them beyond what the employer provides. This needs to be raised at the next meeting, along with the out-of-date wills.

9. Next steps
DF to send the client agreement and fee schedule, the risk questionnaire and a letter of authority so that we can request details of the Marlowe Steelworks scheme and the Aviary Life plan. TH to send payslips and the latest mortgage statement. JH to bring in her documents. Second meeting pencilled in for 18 February to go through a first draft of the plan.

SALTMARSH & FINCH WEALTH LLP - SUITABILITY REPORT
Prepared for: Mr Tobias Hallworth. Prepared by: Daniel Finch, Chartered Financial Planner. Date: 14 March 2025.

1. Why you are receiving this report
You asked us to recommend what to do with the £684,000 you received following your father's death, and to review your existing pensions and ISA. This report sets out our recommendations and the reasons for them. Please read it alongside the illustrations and key information documents enclosed. If anything in the summary of your circumstances is wrong, tell us before you proceed, because our advice depends on it.

2. Your circumstances in brief
You are 43, married to Joanna, with two children aged 11 and 8. You are paid £75,000 a year plus bonus as Principal Data Engineer at Kestrel Ridge Analytics; Joanna is paid about £24,000 for part-time work. Your household spends roughly £4,900 a month. You have a mortgage of £231,000 fixed at 4.19% until June 2028, cash of £38,000 and no other debts. You are both in good health.

3. What you want to achieve
In order of importance you told us: to keep six months' spending instantly available; to be free of the mortgage by the time the fixed rate ends; to be able to stop full-time work at 60; and to see Felix and Martha through university. You do not expect to need the invested capital for at least fifteen years.

4. Your attitude to investment risk and capacity for loss
Your questionnaire of 21 January produced a score of 47 out of 70, which corresponds to profile 6 on our scale of 1 to 10, 'balanced growth'. We discussed what that means in practice: a portfolio of this kind fell by about 19% between January and March 2020 and took around nine months to recover. You told us that you held your existing tracker through that period and did not lose sleep. Joanna is more cautious, and you agreed between you that the mortgage reserve should be kept entirely out of the markets. We assess your capacity for loss as moderate to high: your pay covers your outgoings comfortably, and a 25% fall in the invested amount would delay rather than derail your plans.

5. What we recommend
(a) Hold £30,000 as an emergency reserve in an easy-access account in joint names.
(b) Place £231,000 in a ladder of fixed-term deposits and short-dated gilts maturing by June 2028, earmarked to repay the mortgage when the fixed rate ends, avoiding the early repayment charge of 3% that would apply today.
(c) Use this year's and next year's ISA allowances for you both (£80,000 in total) and invest the remaining £343,000 in a general investment account, phased in over twelve months, in our Balanced Growth 6 model portfolio.
(d) Make a gross pension contribution of £40,000 to your Aviary Life plan (SIPP-448201-TH) this tax year, using carry-forward of unused allowances, which reduces your higher-rate tax bill by about £9,400.

6. Your deferred pension with Marlowe Steelworks
You asked whether you should move this pension into your SIPP so that 'everything is in one place'. We recommend that you do not. The scheme has offered a transfer value of £342,600 in exchange for a guaranteed pension currently estimated at £14,100 a year from age 65, rising with inflation and continuing at half rate to Joanna after your death. The critical yield - the return the transferred sum would have to achieve every year, after charges, to match those benefits - is 6.8%, which we do not consider achievable at profile 6. You have ample flexible savings elsewhere, so the guaranteed element is a valuable foundation rather than a constraint. We will look at this again if the scheme's funding position or your health changes.

7. What it will cost
Our initial fee for this advice and its implementation is £6,850, as set out in the client agreement you signed on 3 February. The ongoing service costs 0.75% a year of the investments we look after. The model portfolio has underlying fund costs of 0.19% a year and the platform charges 0.25% on the first £250,000 and 0.15% above that. The enclosed illustration shows the combined effect of all charges on projected returns.

8. Risks you should understand
The value of investments can fall as well as rise and you may get back less than you put in. Phasing reduces, but does not remove, the risk of investing shortly before a fall. Fixed-term deposits cannot be accessed early without penalty. Tax rules can change, and the value of pension tax relief depends on your circumstances.

9. Your right to change your mind
You can cancel the ISA and general investment account within 14 days, and the pension contribution within 30 days, of receiving the provider's cancellation notice. If the investments have fallen in value during that time you may not get back the full amount.

10. Next steps
If you wish to go ahead, sign and return the enclosed application forms. We will then open the accounts and confirm each stage in writing. Your first review meeting will be in September 2025.

ANNUAL REVIEW - MEETING NOTES
Clients: Marcus Dragomirescu (MD) and Elena Dragomirescu (ED). Adviser: Daniel Finch (DF). Date: 12 June 2025, by video call, 19:30 to 20:45.

1. Portfolio since last review
Value at 31 May 2025 was £318,400 against £289,700 a year earlier, after net contributions of £14,400; a return of 4.8% after all costs, a little behind the composite benchmark (5.3%) because of the underweight to US equities early in the year. The spring sell-off, which prompted ED's e-mail in April, has largely reversed: at its low on 9 April the portfolio was 8.9% below its February peak, and it is now 1.2% above it. We went back over the reasons for staying invested and both said they were glad they had not moved into cash. No change to the strategic allocation in the policy statement: 60% equities, 30% bonds, 10% alternatives and cash. A rebalancing trade was placed on 2 June to bring equities back from 63% to 60%.

2. Changes in circumstances
Their second child, Sofia, was born on 14 March. ED is on maternity leave until January 2026 and then intends to return three days a week, which will cut her pay from £62,000 to about £37,000. MD's role at the freight software firm is unchanged; base £88,000, and his share options vest in 2027. The monthly surplus will fall from about £1,900 to about £600 once ED is back at work part-time and nursery fees for two start. We agreed to reduce the regular investment from £1,200 to £500 a month from September and to revisit in a year.

3. House purchase
They have had an offer accepted on a four-bedroom house in Bishopston at £875,000 and will leave the rented flat in Wren Street when the tenancy ends. Funding: a mortgage of £520,000 agreed in principle with Castlegate Building Society (five-year fixed at 4.34%, 30-year term), £265,000 from their own cash and the house-deposit ISA, and £90,000 given to them by ED's mother, Mrs Constantin. I explained that the lender will ask Mrs Constantin to sign a declaration that the £90,000 is a gift with no interest in the house, and that for our own records we will need her bank statement showing where it was held. The gift is outside UK inheritance tax because she lives in Romania and has no UK assets, so the seven-year rule does not arise. Completion is expected in late August.

4. Protection
Existing arrangements: a joint decreasing term policy for £300,000 taken out in 2019 to match an earlier mortgage plan; MD has death-in-service of four times base through work; ED has none while on leave. With borrowing of £520,000 and two children, there would be a shortfall of roughly £220,000 if MD died and considerably more if ED did. Recommendation to follow in writing: additional decreasing term cover of £220,000 over 30 years on a joint-life, first-death basis, and family income benefit of £2,000 a month on ED's life until Sofia is 21. Indicative combined premium £41 a month. They also asked about critical illness cover; I will include a costed option.

5. School fees
They would like both children to go to an independent secondary school from age 11: Luca in 2030, Sofia in 2036. At today's fees of about £18,000 a year each, rising faster than inflation, the total over fourteen years is of the order of £330,000 in today's terms. The plan is to treat the existing portfolio as the school fees fund for Luca, moving the amount needed for each year into cash and short-dated gilts three years ahead, and to open Junior ISAs for both children with the £9,000 a year that the grandparents have offered. ED asked whether paying fees in advance to the school is worthwhile; I will find out what discount the two schools they like currently offer.

6. Wills and guardians
Their wills date from 2017, before either child was born, and do not name guardians. Both agreed that this is now urgent. I will introduce them to a solicitor. They were reminded that the pre-nuptial agreement provided for a review when their first child arrived, which has never happened.

7. Actions
DF: written protection recommendation by 27 June; school fee discount enquiry; solicitor introduction; update the cashflow model for the new house and the reduced contributions. MD and ED: send the mortgage offer when issued; obtain Mrs Constantin's bank statement and signed gift declaration; confirm nursery costs. Next review: June 2026, or earlier once the purchase completes.

documents.title: Financial plan and cashflow forecast - Henrietta Osgathorpe - May 2025
documents.content:
SALTMARSH & FINCH WEALTH LLP - FINANCIAL PLAN AND CASHFLOW FORECAST
Prepared for Mrs Henrietta Osgathorpe by Daniel Finch, 6 May 2025

1. Summary
You are 63, widowed, and stepped back from day-to-day management of Brambleforth Holdings in February when you sold part of your shareholding. You asked three questions: can you afford to stop drawing a salary altogether, how much can you safely spend, and what would be left for Rupert and Imogen? On the central assumptions below, you can spend £52,000 a year after tax, rising with prices, for the rest of your life without running out, and without relying on any further sale of shares. The plan is robust to the two stress tests we ran. The area that needs attention is not spending but the tax your children would face on your death.

2. What you have
Investment portfolio (general account and ISA) £550,000 at 31 March, plus £480,000 added in March from the share sale and a further £638,000 on deposit awaiting investment or other use; pensions £412,000, untouched; your house, Fell View, about £780,000; the let flat in Leeds, about £215,000, producing £10,250 a year after expenses; and your remaining 500 shares in Brambleforth, which we have valued cautiously at £1.4 million for planning purposes and excluded from the spending forecast. There are no debts.

3. Assumptions
Inflation 2.5% a year. Investment returns after charges: 4.5% for the portfolio, 2.0% for deposits. State Pension of £11,970 a year from age 67. Tax rates, allowances and thresholds as currently legislated and then rising with inflation. Planning horizon to age 97, which only about one woman in ten of your age is expected to reach. Dividends from Brambleforth are treated as a bonus and not relied upon.

4. Spending
Your current outgoings are about £44,000 a year. You asked us to plan for £52,000 to allow for more travel and for the grandchildren's activities. We have assumed that this falls by a fifth in real terms from age 80, as discretionary spending usually does. Until 67 the gap between your rental profit and your spending is met from deposits and the general account, using your capital gains allowance each year; pension withdrawals begin at 67, and only to the extent needed to use the basic-rate band.

5. Results
On the central case your liquid assets rise gently in real terms until your mid-seventies and then level off; at 97 you would still hold about £1.1 million in today's prices, before counting the houses or the shares. A 30% fall in markets in the first year, with no recovery beyond normal returns, reduces that figure to about £640,000 but never threatens your spending. Inflation at 5% for a decade is more damaging than a market fall and would require spending to be trimmed by about £4,000 a year from age 75.

6. Later-life care
We modelled a move into residential nursing care at 85 for four years at £68,000 a year in today's prices, alongside the sale of Fell View at that point. The plan remains comfortably viable: the cost, about £270,000 in today's terms, comes out of capital you are not otherwise forecast to spend. Because your assets are well above the local authority thresholds you would be self-funding throughout, and it is worth knowing that an immediate needs annuity could cap the cost if that ever became a worry. The registered powers of attorney mean that Rupert and Imogen could manage this for you if necessary.

7. Tax on your death
This is where the plan is weakest. If you died today, about £2.66 million of your assets would be exposed to inheritance tax: the portfolio, the deposits, Fell View and the Leeds flat. Your pensions currently fall outside the calculation, and we have assumed that business relief continues to cover the Brambleforth shares. After two nil-rate bands (your own and your late husband's unused one), roughly £2.0 million would be taxable at 40%: an estimated bill of about £805,000. The additional allowance for a home left to children is tapered away completely for estates of this size.
Three things would reduce it: (a) regular gifts out of surplus income, which are immediately exempt if documented - you have roughly £20,000 a year of genuine surplus; (b) larger lifetime gifts or further settlements into the family trust, which fall out of account after seven years; (c) leaving the pensions untouched for as long as practical. We also suggest obtaining a price for whole-of-life cover written in trust to meet part of the bill, though at 63 the premiums are substantial. Your plans to live in Portugal do not remove the exposure in the near term.

8. Recommendations
Stop drawing salary from July; invest £400,000 of the deposit balance in the existing portfolio over six months and keep the remainder as a three-year spending reserve; begin a documented pattern of gifts of £1,500 a month in total to Rupert and Imogen; meet the solicitor with us in June to consider a second settlement; review this plan each May or on any major change.

SALTMARSH & FINCH WEALTH LLP - QUARTERLY INVESTMENT COMMENTARY, FIRST QUARTER 2025
For clients invested in our model portfolios. Written by the Investment Committee, 11 April 2025.

1. The quarter in brief
After two strong years, global share prices went sideways in January and February and fell in March. Developed-market equities ended the quarter 2.9% lower in sterling terms. The pattern underneath was more interesting than the headline: European and UK shares rose, while the large American technology companies that had led the market for most of 2023 and 2024 fell by more than 10%. Bonds did their job, with UK government bonds returning 0.7% and investment-grade corporate bonds 1.1%. A balanced portfolio therefore finished the quarter roughly where it started, which will not have been obvious to anyone reading the headlines in the last week of March.

2. What drove markets
Three things mattered. First, trade policy: the announcement of new US tariffs, and the uncertainty about how far they would go, led companies to delay investment decisions and analysts to trim profit forecasts. Second, a change of mood about artificial intelligence spending, after several large firms signalled that capital expenditure would grow more slowly than investors had assumed. Third, Europe: Germany's decision to relax its borrowing limits to fund defence and infrastructure lifted growth expectations across the continent and pushed European shares to their best relative quarter in a decade.

3. Interest rates and inflation
The Bank of England cut Bank Rate by a quarter point in February, to 4.5%, and held in March. UK inflation remains above target at 2.8%, largely because of services prices and regulated household bills, and we expect it to rise a little further over the summer before easing. Markets price two more cuts this year; we think that is reasonable. For savers, the practical consequence is that the best easy-access rates have slipped below 4.5% and one-year fixed rates below 4.3%. For borrowers, five-year fixed mortgage rates have changed little.

4. Regions and sectors
United States: the weakest major market over the quarter, though after a long period of leadership valuations remain higher than elsewhere. United Kingdom: helped by banks, defence and a low starting valuation; the main index is up 5% year to date. Europe: strong, as described above. Japan: flat in local currency, modestly negative in sterling. Emerging markets: slightly positive, with China recovering and India weak. Within bonds, shorter maturities outperformed longer ones as investors demanded more compensation for lending to governments for long periods.

5. How the model portfolios performed
Over the three months to 31 March the returns after fund costs were: Cautious 3, +0.4%; Balanced 5, -0.6%; Balanced Growth 6, -1.1%; Growth 8, -2.0%. Over five years the same portfolios have returned +14.8%, +29.5%, +37.2% and +51.6% respectively. The figures do not include platform or advice charges, and past performance is not a guide to future returns.

6. Changes we have made
The committee made three changes on 2 April, applied to all models at the scheduled rebalance. First, we trimmed the US equity index fund by three percentage points in the growth-oriented models and added the proceeds to the equal-weighted global fund, reducing the dependence on a handful of very large companies. Second, we shortened the average maturity of the UK government bond holding from eleven years to seven by switching half of it into a short-dated gilt fund. Third, we introduced a 3% position in a physically backed gold exchange-traded commodity, funded from cash and absolute-return funds. Gold has no yield and we do not hold it for its recent price rise; we hold it because it has tended to keep its value in periods when both shares and bonds fall together, as they did in 2022, and because central banks continue to add to their reserves.

7. Looking ahead
We do not forecast markets and are sceptical of those who claim to. Profits are still growing, employment is high and interest rates are falling, which is normally a supportive combination. Against that, policy is unusually unpredictable. Our response is to stay diversified, keep costs low and rebalance on schedule rather than on headlines.

8. Important information
This commentary is for general information and is not personal advice. The value of investments and the income from them can fall as well as rise, and you may not get back the amount you invested. If your circumstances have changed, please speak to your adviser.

documents.content:
SOURCE OF WEALTH MEMORANDUM
Subject: Mr Aurelian Vasilache-Stroe (born 1968, Romanian national, UK resident since 2022)
Prepared by: Daniel Finch. Reviewed by: Margaret Saltmarsh, Money Laundering Reporting Officer. Date: 9 May 2025. Classification: confidential - compliance file.

1. Purpose
Mr Vasilache-Stroe proposes to place approximately £2.5 million under our management. Because of the size of the relationship, the cross-border history and the family connection described in section 6, the firm's policy requires a documented understanding of how his overall wealth was built up, in addition to the origin of the specific sum being invested. This memorandum records what we were told, what we have seen and what we concluded.

2. Background
Mr Vasilache-Stroe was born in Ploiesti and graduated in mechanical engineering from the Polytechnic University of Bucharest in 1991. He is married with two adult children, both of whom live in London. He and his wife have held UK residence permits since March 2022 and live in Richmond.

3. Early career
From 1991 to 1998 he worked as a maintenance engineer and later depot manager for the state railway freight operator. From 1998 to 2005 he was operations director of a privately owned haulage firm in Constanta. He describes his savings on leaving that job as 'a car and enough for a deposit', which is consistent with salaried employment in Romania at the time; no significant wealth is attributed to this period.

4. The company
In 2006 he founded Carpathia Freight Systems SRL with a partner, each holding 50%, to provide container tracking and customs paperwork for forwarders using the port of Constanta. The company grew with Romania's accession to the European Union in 2007: turnover rose from the equivalent of EUR 0.4 million in 2007 to EUR 11.8 million in 2019, and it employed 140 people at its peak. He bought out his partner in 2014 for EUR 600,000, financed by a bank loan repaid from dividends by 2017. We have seen audited accounts for 2015 to 2020, which show cumulative dividends to him of EUR 2.1 million over that period, and the corresponding entries in his personal bank statements.

5. The sale
In September 2021 he sold 100% of the company to Nordhaven Logistics Group AB, a listed Swedish freight technology company, for EUR 7.4 million: EUR 6.2 million in cash at completion and EUR 1.2 million deferred for two years, which was paid in full in October 2023. We have seen the share sale agreement, the buyer's stock exchange announcement of 14 September 2021, the notary's completion record and bank statements showing receipt of both payments. Romanian tax on the gain was paid in 2022; the tax receipt is on file. This transaction accounts for roughly three quarters of his present net worth.

6. Political connection
His wife's brother has been a member of the Romanian Chamber of Deputies since 2020. Mr Vasilache-Stroe has never held public office, was not a supplier to the state after 1998, and the company's customer list for 2015 to 2020, which we reviewed, contains no public bodies. Screening shows no adverse media. He is nevertheless treated as politically exposed by association and the relationship has been escalated accordingly; see the separate enhanced due diligence memo.

7. Property and other assets
He owns three apartments in Bucharest bought between 2009 and 2016 for a total of about EUR 410,000 (land registry extracts seen), two of which are let, and the family's house in Richmond bought in 2022 for £1.85 million without borrowing (completion statement and solicitor's letter seen). Cash and investments of about EUR 3.3 million are held with a bank in Vienna, from which the proposed transfer will be made. He has received no gifts or legacies of any size.

8. Assessment
The account he gives is coherent, consistent over two meetings and supported by independent documents at each material step. Total wealth of about £6.5 million is in proportion to the dividends and sale consideration evidenced. The residual concerns are jurisdictional and the political connection, neither of which is aggravated by anything we have found.

9. Decision
Risk rating: high, because of the political exposure. Approved to proceed by Margaret Saltmarsh on 12 May 2025, subject to: funds to be received only from the Vienna account in his own name; annual review of this memorandum; any third-party payment in or out to be referred to the MLRO before it is processed.

documents.title: Fact find - Caleb Winterbourne - 2 April 2025
documents.content:
CONFIDENTIAL FACT FIND
Client: Caleb Winterbourne. Completed by: Daniel Finch at a meeting on 2 April 2025 and from documents supplied afterwards.

A. Personal details
Full name: Caleb Elias Winterbourne. Date of birth: 19 August 1985. Nationality: United States. Marital status: single, no children. Partner: Dr Niamh Corrigan (Irish national), not financially dependent. Health: good; non-smoker. Arrived in the UK on 6 January 2025 on a Skilled Worker visa sponsored by his employer, valid for five years. Currently renting a flat in Cambridge on a twelve-month tenancy; intends to buy within two years if the posting is extended. Previous home: Portland, Oregon.

B. Employment
Employer: Halcyon Wharf Robotics Ltd (UK subsidiary of Halcyon Wharf Robotics Inc.). Role: Director of Perception Engineering. UK base salary £165,000 plus annual bonus target of 20% and restricted stock units in the US parent vesting quarterly (about $60,000 a year at the current share price). Relocation allowance of £25,000 paid in January. He is a member of the UK group pension plan with a 6% employer contribution but has opted out for now on the advice of his US accountant - see section E.

C. Assets
401(k) with his former US employer plan: $418,000, invested mainly in a target-date fund; no further contributions possible. Roth IRA: $74,000. Taxable brokerage account with Redwood Ledger Brokerage: $236,000, mostly US index funds, plus vested employer shares worth about $95,000. House in Portland, bought 2018, value about $640,000, let since February through a managing agent at $3,100 a month. UK current account: £31,000. US checking and savings: $42,000.

D. Liabilities
Mortgage on the Portland house: $312,000 outstanding, 30-year fixed at 3.1%. No other borrowing. Credit cards are cleared monthly.

E. Tax position
This is the dominant planning issue. As a US citizen he remains taxable in the United States on his worldwide income wherever he lives, and must continue to file Form 1040 each year together with the foreign bank account report (FBAR) for his UK accounts. He became UK tax resident on arrival and is using the four-year foreign income and gains regime, so his US rental and investment income is not taxed in the UK for now, but his UK salary is taxed in both countries with relief by foreign tax credit. Consequences for anything we recommend: (1) UK-domiciled funds, investment trusts and most ISA investments are treated by the US as passive foreign investment companies and taxed punitively - he should not buy them; (2) an ISA has no tax advantage for US purposes; (3) the UK workplace pension is broadly recognised under the treaty, and opting out is probably costing him the employer contribution for no good reason - to be confirmed with a dual-qualified tax adviser; (4) any UK adviser or platform must be willing to accept US persons and report under FATCA.

F. Protection
Death-in-service of four times salary and income protection of 75% of salary after 26 weeks through the UK employer. A US term policy of $500,000 remains in force until 2040. Private medical cover is provided for him and his partner by the employer.

G. Wills and succession
He signed a revocable living trust and pour-over will in Oregon in 2019, naming his sister as successor trustee and his parents and sister as beneficiaries. He has no UK will. His partner is not provided for. He was unaware that a UK-situated house would fall under English succession rules. Action: refer to a solicitor with US and English expertise once a UK purchase is in prospect.

H. Objectives
In his words: 'do not let the move wreck my finances.' Specifically: keep his investments compliant in both countries; decide whether to keep or sell the Portland house; build a deposit of £150,000 for a UK purchase by 2027; continue to save about 20% of gross pay for the long term; understand what happens if he stays in the UK permanently.

I. Attitude to risk
Experienced investor; has held equity index funds since his twenties and added to them in 2020 and 2022. Questionnaire result: profile 7 of 10. Capacity for loss high given age, earnings and absence of dependants. Deposit fund to be kept in cash and short-dated government bonds regardless.

J. Documents received
US passport (copy certified), visa vignette and residence permit, tenancy agreement, three UK payslips, latest brokerage and plan statements, 2023 US tax return.

documents.title: File note - vulnerability and capacity review - Winifred Ashdown-Pryce
documents.content:
FILE NOTE - VULNERABLE CLIENT REVIEW
Client: Mrs Winifred Ashdown-Pryce (aged 84). Author: Daniel Finch. Date of meeting: 27 February 2025, at her home in Otley. Also present: her nephew, Jasper Pryce. Note written the same afternoon.

1. Why this note exists
At the annual review in November I recorded that Mrs Ashdown-Pryce seemed less sure of herself than in previous years. Since then she has telephoned the office four times to ask for her balance, on two occasions twice in the same morning, and in January she asked our administrator who I was. Her nephew rang me on 12 February to say that the family had concerns of their own and to ask for a meeting. This note records what I saw, what I was told, and what we have changed as a result. It should be read before anyone takes an instruction from her.

2. What I observed
She was welcoming, well dressed and the house was in good order. She knew who I was once reminded, and talked fluently about her late husband and about the garden. She could not tell me roughly what her investments were worth, or what the monthly payment from the portfolio was for, and asked three times in forty minutes whether her money was 'still safe'. When I explained the regular withdrawal she understood, agreed it should continue, and ten minutes later had no memory of the explanation. She became briefly distressed when she could not find her reading glasses, which were on the table in front of her.

3. Medical position
Mr Pryce told me, with her agreement, that her GP referred her to the memory clinic in the autumn and that Alzheimer's disease at an early stage was confirmed in November 2024. She has been prescribed donepezil and will be seen again in May. The consultant's letter, which I was shown, says that she is able to make everyday decisions with support but is likely to find complex financial matters increasingly difficult. Nobody has suggested that she lacks capacity in general, and I have not treated her as though she does: the question is whether she can understand, retain and weigh a particular decision at the time it has to be made.

4. Who can give instructions
She signed a lasting power of attorney for property and financial affairs in 2019, registered the same year, appointing Mr Pryce and her solicitor, Mrs Odette Lanyon of Lanyon Marsh, to act jointly for decisions about selling her house and separately for everything else. I have seen the registered document and taken a certified copy; both attorneys' identities were verified in 2019 and Mr Pryce's has been refreshed today. With her consent, given in front of me and recorded here, the attorneys will from now on be copied into all correspondence and Mr Pryce will attend every meeting. Where she is able to decide something herself she will continue to do so, and we will confirm it in writing to her and to him.

5. Money and care
Carers now visit twice a day at a cost of about £2,400 a month, paid from her current account. Her pensions bring in £1,850 a month after tax, so the existing withdrawal of £1,000 a month no longer covers the gap. We agreed to raise it to £1,600 from April. At that rate, and allowing for costs rising, the portfolio of £486,000 lasts well beyond age 100 on cautious assumptions, even before the house is considered. If she later needs full-time residential care the figures should be rerun.

6. Investments
The portfolio is in our Balanced 5 model. Given the shorter horizon, the higher withdrawals and the need for her attorneys to be comfortable with what they are overseeing, I recommended a switch to Cautious 3 and a cash reserve equal to two years of withdrawals. She said, 'I don't want any excitement,' and Mr Pryce agreed. A short suitability letter will go to both of them and Mrs Lanyon before anything is done.

7. Safeguards put in place today
Vulnerability marker added to her record. No instruction to be accepted from her by telephone alone; staff to call Mr Pryce back on the number we hold. No change of bank details without both attorneys' written confirmation. Paper valuations to continue because she likes to receive them, with a copy to Mr Pryce by e-mail. Her daughter-in-law in Canada is not an attorney and should not be given information.

8. Review
Next contact in three months, after the clinic appointment, and a full review in six. Sooner if the family or the carers report a change.

documents.title: Retirement income options report - Gideon Marchbanks - 2 May 2025
documents.content:
SALTMARSH & FINCH WEALTH LLP - RETIREMENT INCOME OPTIONS REPORT
Prepared for Mr Gideon Marchbanks by Daniel Finch, 2 May 2025

1. Where you are
You will be 65 on 14 July and plan to finish at the council on 31 July after thirty-one years. Ruth, who is 62, intends to carry on at the library two days a week until she is 66. You have two personal pensions built up before and alongside your council service: £338,000 with Aviary Life and £174,000 with Pennant Mutual, £512,000 in total. Your local government pension will pay £19,600 a year from August, rising with prices, and your State Pension of about £11,900 starts at 66. Ruth's own pensions will add roughly £13,000 from 66 and 67. You have £86,000 in cash ISAs, £22,000 in premium bonds and a mortgage of £74,500 on which the fixed rate ended in March.

2. What you need
You have told us that the two of you spend about £3,300 a month and would like £3,900 for the first ten years so that you can travel while you are fit. Your guaranteed pensions cover the essentials from the day you stop work; the personal pensions are there to fund the extras, to bridge the year before your State Pension, and to provide a reserve. That is a strong position, and it shapes everything below.

3. The options we considered
(a) Buying an annuity with the whole fund. On 2 May the best quotation we obtained was £9,870 a year for each £150,000 on a level, single-life basis with a five-year guarantee, or £6,410 if it rises by 3% a year and continues at two-thirds to Ruth. An annuity is simple and cannot run out, but it is irreversible, and you already have more guaranteed income than most people.
(b) Flexi-access drawdown for the whole fund. The money stays invested and you draw what you need. This gives control and leaves whatever is unspent to the family, but the income is not guaranteed and depends on investment returns and on your own discipline.
(c) Taking lump sums as required directly from the existing plans. Possible with Aviary Life but not with Pennant Mutual, and the tax treatment is clumsy.
(d) A combination.

4. Tax-free cash and the mortgage
A quarter of the fund, £128,000, can be taken tax-free. We recommend that you take it in full at the outset and use £74,500 of it to repay the mortgage. The loan now costs you 7.24% on the lender's standard variable rate, far more than the cash could safely earn, and clearing it reduces your monthly outgoings by £612. The remaining £53,500 would top up your cash reserve to roughly two years of extra spending. You asked whether it would be better to leave the tax-free amount invested and draw it gradually; in other circumstances it might, but not while you are paying that rate of interest.

5. Our recommendation
Transfer both plans into a single drawdown account. Take the tax-free cash as described. From the remaining £384,000, draw £7,200 a year (£600 a month) from August, which with your council pension keeps you within the basic-rate band, and review the level each spring. Invest the drawdown fund in our Balanced 5 model portfolio, with three years of planned withdrawals held in cash and short-dated gilts inside the account so that you are never forced to sell shares after a fall. We do not recommend an annuity now. We do recommend revisiting the question at 75, when rates for your age will be considerably higher and simplicity may matter more to you both.

6. Will it last?
On our central assumptions (returns of 4% a year after charges, inflation of 2.5%) withdrawals of £7,200 rising with prices leave about £350,000 in today's terms at age 90. If returns are two percentage points lower throughout, the fund still lasts beyond 95. If you wanted to draw twice as much it would be exhausted at about 88, at which point your guaranteed pensions would still exceed your essential spending.

7. If you die
Money left in drawdown does not form part of your estate under the present rules and can pass to anyone you nominate. You have completed a nomination in favour of Ruth, and then Callum and Hannah equally. If you die before 75 the beneficiaries pay no income tax on what they draw; after 75 they pay tax at their own rates. The Government has announced that unused pension funds will be brought within inheritance tax from April 2027; for a couple this does not bite on the first death, but we will need to look again at the order in which you spend your savings.

8. Charges
Initial advice and implementation: £5,760, deducted from the fund. Ongoing: our service 0.75% a year, platform 0.25%, underlying funds 0.17%. A full illustration is enclosed.

9. Risks
Drawdown funds can fall in value. High withdrawals, poor returns in the early years or living much longer than expected could all reduce what is available later. The tax rules described here may change.

10. What happens next
If you agree, sign the transfer and drawdown application forms. Transfers typically take three to five weeks; we will time the tax-free payment to arrive shortly before your mortgage lender's next payment date.
